title: Deterministic competitive ratio for matching with delays
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\rho(n)\) for online minimum-cost perfect matching with linear waiting costs on a known \(n\)-point metric. The ratio must depend only on \(n\), uniformly over the number and timing of requests and all distances in the metric.
why: This question measures the unavoidable cost of making irrevocable pairings while deciding how long to wait for future demand. A sharp deterministic ratio would separate the value of randomization from the difficulty of balancing spatial matching cost and elapsed waiting time in general metric spaces.
status_note: The n-parameter deterministic gap is open in the 2020 source. Checks through 13 September 2026 found the major new polylogarithmic m-bound and results for other delay models, but no matching characterization of the stated n-only function. This bounded review does not exhaustively certify current openness.

category_assignment.reason: The original source asks for competitive deterministic online metric matching with waiting costs.

importance.reason: A central deterministic-versus-randomized frontier for online decisions with delay, requiring a uniform guarantee over arbitrary metric geometry and unbounded request streams.

sentences: Matching with delays pairs arriving requests while charging both the distance between partners and the time each request waits.
The selected question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as a function of the number of points in a known metric.
The guarantee must hold for any finite even request sequence, with no bound on its length or advance notice of its end.
A SODA 2026 algorithm gives a polylogarithmic ratio in the number of requests, which does not alone determine the ratio uniformly in metric size.
Matching bounds in the metric-size parameter would clarify the value of randomization in balancing spatial cost against waiting.

definitions: A metric on \([n]\) is a symmetric map \(d:[n]^2\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) that vanishes exactly on equal points and satisfies the triangle inequality. The algorithm knows the whole metric before requests arrive. An input is any finite sequence of \(m\geq2\) distinctly identified requests, with \(m\) even, locations \(v_i\in[n]\), and arrival times \(0\leq a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_m<\infty\). Repeated locations and simultaneous arrivals are allowed; all requests at a given time are revealed before decisions made at that time. The algorithm does not know \(m\), future arrivals or an end-of-input time. It can irrevocably match two currently unmatched requests \(i,j\) at any real time \(t\geq\max(a_i,a_j)\), paying \(d(v_i,v_j)+(t-a_i)+(t-a_j)\). Every request must eventually be matched at a finite time on every finite even input. There are no colors, capacities or restrictions on the pairs. A deterministic online algorithm is a causal rule: its decisions through time \(t\) depend only on the known metric and requests revealed through \(t\). Computation and memory are unrestricted and uncharged, and decisions may be scheduled between arrivals. The total cost is the sum of all pair costs. The offline optimum, knowing the entire sequence, is \[\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)=\min_{\text{perfect matchings }P}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in P}\bigl(d(v_i,v_j)+|a_i-a_j|\bigr),\] since an offline pair can be matched when its later request arrives. Define \(r(d)=\inf\{C\geq1:\exists A\ \forall\sigma,\ \operatorname{cost}_A(d,\sigma)\leq C\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)\}\), with infinity if no finite ratio is possible, and \(\rho(n)=\sup_{d\text{ on }[n]}r(d)\), for \(n\geq2\). The algorithm in the infimum may depend on the entire metric. This is pure multiplicative competitiveness, with no additive constant; an input of optimum zero must incur zero cost. Infima over algorithms and suprema over metrics need not be attained. For deterministic rules, allowing an adaptive adversary does not change the requirement over all inputs.
answer_criterion: Give a noncircular rate \(G(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG(n)\leq\rho(n)\leq CG(n)\) for universal positive constants and all sufficiently large \(n\). Upper bounds must hold for every metric and all finite even request sequences; lower bounds must apply to every deterministic online algorithm in the specified model. Use approaching bounds if an extremum is not attained. A ratio depending on the request count, a randomized expected guarantee, or a theorem only for the line or uniform metrics does not determine this function.

context_blocks.text: Azar’s 2020 problem statement asks to close the deterministic competitiveness gap, expressed either through the metric size or through the number of requests. This card explicitly selects the known finite metric and metric-size parameter. Its separately mentioned red-blue matching variant is not part of the target.

The source reports an \(O(n)\) deterministic upper bound and a lower bound of order \(\log n/\log\log n\), the latter holding even against randomized algorithms. It also reports an \(O(\log n)\) randomized upper bound. These are dated source bounds and should not be conflated with a deterministic logarithmic theorem.

Dufay and Wattenhofer’s SODA 2026 result gives a deterministic \(O(\log^5 m)\)-competitive algorithm even when the metric and request count are unknown. It substantially improves the source’s request-count comparison. However, \(m\) can be arbitrarily large at fixed \(n\), so that displayed bound alone gives no uniform polylogarithmic bound in \(n\).

Gan, Sun and Umboh’s September 2026 paper studies general size-dependent delay rates and nonlinear convex waiting costs. Its tight deterministic result for the broader size-dependent model is not a matching lower bound for this fixed linear-per-request delay objective. Its uniform-metric results also have a narrower geometric scope.

Waiting may expose a nearby future partner, but it also accumulates cost on every unmatched request. The metric can have arbitrary scale and aspect ratio, making the information available from future arrivals essential even when computation of a present-day best matching is free.
